strengths: A highly novel paradigm shift: directly tokenizing raw 4D motion (3D space + 1D time) instead of relying on lossy 2D-rendered pose images, which effectively resolves the typical issue of pixel-level mismatch and spatial distortion.

Well-designed technical components, such as the 4D Motion Tokenizer (4DMoT) to quantize 3D SMPL sequences, and the 4D Rotary Positional Encoding (4D RoPE) that successfully preserves spatio-temporal relationships in the tokenized space.
Very strong empirical results: achieving an outstanding FID-VID of 6.98 on the TikTok dataset, which represents a massive improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods.
Identity preservation is handled efficiently via a repeat-and-concatenate strategy in self-attention, avoiding the computational redundancy of a separate ReferenceNet.
Excellent qualitative results showing robust generalization across diverse character proportions, stylized non-human structures, and complex motions.
weaknesses: High dependency on the accuracy of 3D SMPL pose estimators; if the estimator fails or produces noisy estimates (e.g., under extreme occlusion or non-standard viewpoints), it is unclear how robustly the model behaves.
The evaluation is somewhat narrow, with quantitative metrics reported almost exclusively on the TikTok dataset; including additional benchmarks would make the evaluation more comprehensive.
Significant computational requirements (7B parameters, trained on H100 GPUs), which might limit its reproducibility or adoption in resource-constrained environments.

strengths: Pioneers a new paradigm by directly modeling raw 4D motion sequences (3D joints over time) as discrete tokens, rather than relying on 2D-rendered pose images (skeletons/depth/mesh renderings) which often suffer from pixel-level copying artifacts and scale mismatches.
Introduces 4DMoT (a VQ-VAE based motion tokenizer) and a custom-designed 4D RoPE (temporal + 3D spatial) that preserves the underlying physical structure of the motion despite discrete quantization.
Replaces complex ReferenceNet branches with a simpler and more efficient repeat-and-concatenate strategy in the DiT self-attention, preserving character identity with lower computational cost.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on the TikTok benchmark, significantly outperforming previous methods in FID-VID (6.98 vs 20.64 for the next best) and visual fidelity.
Provides thorough and convincing qualitative results, including cross-style generation (anime, pixel art, ink drawings) and extreme shape deformation cases (e.g., muscles/non-standard proportions).
Includes a detailed ablation study on tokenizer quantization, different positional encoding variations (dynamic, learnable, spatial/temporal only), and classifier-free guidance scales.
weaknesses: The framework relies heavily on 3D pose estimators (like NLF-Pose) to obtain the driving 3D SMPL parameters at inference. If the 3D pose estimator struggles with occlusions or fast movements in the driving video, the quality of downstream tokenization and animation may degrade.
The method is restricted to single-person animation and struggles to handle extreme, non-human cartoon body proportions (as shown in the limitations) due to statistical centralization in 4D RoPE.
High computational cost: training requires 8 H100 GPUs for several days, and inference takes about 90 seconds on a single H100 for a short clip, which limits real-time application.

strengths: Innovative core motivation: Decoupling motion from visual representations by tokenizing raw 4D motion (3D joint coordinates over time) instead of relying on 2D skeleton/dense mesh rendering. This effectively addresses shape-mismatch issues (e.g., Hulk or highly stylized characters) and avoids pixel-level copy artifacts.

A well-designed, two-stage framework: 4DMoT (motion VQ-VAE) effectively quantizes joint sequences into unified tokens, and MV-DiT successfully processes these tokens via 4D Motion Attention combined with a bespoke 4D RoPE (1D temporal and 3D spatial joint coordinates).

Efficient design choices: Concatenating reference image latents directly to video latents in the DiT self-attention avoids the computational overhead of maintaining a separate, heavy ReferenceNet, while still preserving identity successfully.

Outstanding experimental results: MTVCrafter significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the TikTok benchmark, bringing the FID-VID metric down to an impressive 6.98 (compared to >20.0 for previous methods).
Strong qualitative demonstration of generalization to diverse styles (anime, pixel art, ink drawings), half/full-body transitions, and multiple characters.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on 3D pose estimation accuracy: The quality of the animation relies entirely on the precision of the estimated SMPL coordinates from the driven video. If joint estimation fails or is noisy (e.g., in complex or occluded scenarios), the model lacks pixel-level image-driven fallback structures.

Limitations on multi-person animation: Although Figure 1 displays multiple characters, they share identical target poses. As noted in the Appendix, the current pipeline cannot support multi-person animations with independent, distinct poses. This single-person training constraint should be discussed more prominently in the main text.

High computational requirement: Training a 7B-parameter DiT with 42 added motion-attention layers requires significant hardware resources (8 H100 days), which might limit reproducibility and adaptation by researchers with fewer computational resources.

strengths: Innovative paradigm shift: Shifting the pose-guided video generation framework from relying on 2D-rendered images (skeletons, depth, meshes) to directly modeling 4D raw motion (3D joint coordinates over time) via tokenization.

Well-designed technical components: The 4D Motion Tokenizer (4DMoT) using differential coordinates and the 4D Rotary Position Embedding (4D RoPE) are logically sound, well-formulated, and successfully address spatial-temporal alignment in video diffusion transformers.

Compelling qualitative results and zero-shot generalization: MTVCraft demonstrates impressive generalization, allowing the animation of arbitrary characters, non-human entities (e.g., animals, cartoon characters), and inanimate objects while maintaining structural consistency.

Comprehensive evaluation and scalability: The model is quantitatively validated on the TikTok and Fashion benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, scaling experiments from 6B (CogVideoX) to 18B (Wan-2.1) demonstrate the approach's robustness and scalability.
weaknesses: Sparse representation limitations: The tokenizer relies on 24 SMPL joint coordinates. This sparse representation lacks detailed human keypoints for hands/fingers and facial expressions, which are crucial for expressive character animation. While 2D-rendered methods (like DWPose or SMPL-X mesh renders) can naturally convey detailed facial/hand cues, the proposed 4D tokens struggle here, as acknowledged in the limitations.

Implicit mapping for non-human subjects: The paper showcases impressive results animating non-human characters (such as Stitch, SpongeBob, and a Shiba Inu). However, it is not fully clear how the model maps human-centric 4D SMPL joint tokens to the completely different topologies and skeleton structures of these non-human characters. A more detailed explanation of this cross-domain mapping mechanism would strengthen the paper.

Strong dependency on 3D pose estimation: Since the input relies on raw 3D joints, the quality of the video generation is highly dependent on the accuracy of the upstream 3D pose estimator (e.g., NLF-Pose). Severe self-occlusions, rapid motions, or atypical camera viewpoints in the driving video might lead to erratic 3D joint estimations, which will directly degrade the animation.

Potential copy-paste artifacts from identity insertion: The model uses a simple repeat-and-concatenate strategy (Eq. 3) to inject the reference image. While computationally efficient compared to a separate ReferenceNet, this design choice can sometimes cause background bleeding or copy-paste artifacts when the target pose deviates dramatically from the reference pose.

strengths: Innovative core concept that shifts the paradigm from pixel-level 2D pose image guidance (like skeletons or depth maps) to tokenized 4D motion (3D joint trajectories over time). This effectively resolves geometric misalignment and pixel-level copying artifacts common in existing methods.

Well-designed technical components, specifically the 4D Motion Tokenizer (4DMoT) which uses differential joint coordinates to capture relative motion dynamics, and the 4D Rotary Position Embedding (4D RoPE) which structurally aligns spatial-temporal dimensions between vision and motion tokens.

Outstanding zero-shot generalization capabilities. The model is able to animate diverse non-human characters, animals, and objects using human driving motion without retraining, highlighting the robust decoupling of appearance and motion.

Comprehensive experimental validation and scalability. The framework is tested on standard TikTok and Fashion benchmarks, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance, and scales successfully to modern massive DiT backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B).
weaknesses: Limited expressiveness in detailed areas like hands and face. Since the tokenizer relies on standard SMPL joints (24 coordinates), it lacks dense keypoints for hands and facial expressions, making it less competitive for highly expressive character animations compared to SMPL-X or dense 2D pose guided methods.

High dependence on the quality of front-end 3D pose estimation. Errors or jitter in the estimated 3D joints (especially during complex actions or occlusions) will propagate directly to the generated videos. A discussion or analysis on how sensitive the generation is to noisy 3D joints would improve completeness.

Lack of analysis regarding inference latency and computational overhead. Inserting 4D Motion Attention blocks into massive DiT architectures adds computational steps. The authors should provide a quantitative comparison of the runtime overhead introduced by 4DMoT and MV-DiT relative to 2D control baselines.

strengths: Novel perspective on motion representation: Instead of using typical 2D-rendered representations (skeletons, depth, or mesh), the paper proposes a discrete 4D motion tokenizer (4DMoT) to represent 3D joint coordinate sequences as tokens, decoupling motion from absolute scale and body shape.

Innovative architectural designs: The introduction of a dedicated 4D Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that spans temporal (1D) and spatial (3D) coordinates allows for structured, geometrically compatible interactions between motion and vision tokens in the attention layers.

Strong scalability and empirical performance: The authors demonstrate the versatility of their approach by applying it to two large-scale video backbones: CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B. The quantitative results on the TikTok and Fashion benchmarks show a clear improvement over current SOTA methods (e.g., FVD decreases significantly).

Impressive qualitative results: The visual results show high-fidelity character generation, good identity preservation (without an explicit reference network), and the ability to animate diverse styles (e.g., anime, sketches) and even non-human objects/animals.
weaknesses: Incomplete writing and empty placeholders: The abstract contains blank spaces where the project page and commercial deployment URLs should be ('Our project page is available at . A scaled version...'). Such placeholders make the submission look unpolished and rushed.

Confusing figure referencing: In Section 3.3, the text refers to Figure 6 ('As shown in Figure 6, the scaled version...'), but Figure 6 is located in the Appendix on page 19. The main body of the paper should explicitly guide the reader to the Appendix when referencing figures placed there.

Lack of clarity on non-human animation: The paper claims to animate non-human objects and animals (e.g., dogs, fire hydrants in Figure 16). However, the underlying motion tokens are derived from human SMPL joint coordinates. It should be explicitly clarified how these human coordinates are mapped/transferred to non-human skeletons or meshes, as they do not naturally share the same skeletal structure.

Coarse motion representations: Since 4DMoT uses 24 standard SMPL joints, it naturally lacks finer structures such as hands and facial expressions. The authors acknowledge the hand control limitation in Appendix D, but this coarse representation remains a physical bottleneck for realistic close-up animations.
